## KEY FINDINGS

### 1. What conservative nTOS protocols actually target — and what they do not specify

**O'Sullivan 2026 is the definitive answer, and it is unflattering.** 29 of 1381 studies met eligibility. Exercise appeared in 17/19 (90%) of programmes. Within that:
- **Stretching (n=15).** Main targets: **scalenes and pectoralis (n=10)**.
- **Strengthening (n=14).** Main targets: **scapula (n=9), trapezius and serratus anterior (n=5)**.
- Neural mobility (n=7), posture improvement (n=13), manual therapy (n=10), adjuncts (n=8), activity modification (n=7).

So the brief's premise is confirmed at the level of *muscle selection*: these protocols are built around scapular stabilisers, trapezius, serratus anterior, and scalene/pec minor lengthening. **But the premise fails at the level of muscle *quality*.** The review's own conclusion: *"The reporting of rehabilitation techniques for NTOS is generally poor, particularly regarding treatment intensity. There is an essential need for a standardised and reproducible rehabilitation intervention for NTOS to be developed."*

**Translation for the brief: the literature does not tell you whether these protocols prescribe endurance or maximal strength, because they do not report dose.** There is no published nTOS protocol specifying sets, reps, loads, or time-under-tension in a way that would let you classify it as endurance training. Anyone asserting "the protocols target endurance specifically" is reading intent into silence.

**Watson Part 2** describes the core as *"the graded restoration of scapula control, movement, and positioning at rest and through movement,"* with adjuncts of *"restoration of humeral head control, isolated strengthening of weak shoulder muscles, taping, and other manual therapy techniques."* This is **motor-control language, not endurance language**. The abstract does not mention diaphragmatic breathing or deep neck flexors. (Abstract-level verification only; full text may add dose detail.)

**Hooper Part 2** gives no protocol and no success rates — it is a clinical-reasoning paper: *"The clinician uses clinical examination results to design a rehabilitation program that focuses on correcting specific problems that were previously identified."*

**Success rates — a floor and a ceiling, with the truth unknown:**

| Study | n | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Novak 1995 | 42 | 25 improved / 10 same / 7 worse (~60%). Only 16/42 back to full work + recreation. Poor outcome linked to obesity, workers' comp, concomitant carpal/cubital tunnel (all p<.04). |
| Lindgren 1997 | 119 | 88% satisfied at mean 24.6 mo; ROM normalised in 8/10; 73% returned to work. Uncontrolled, subjective endpoint, inpatient-selected. |
| Balderman 2019 | 150 | All got a 6-week PT trial. **40 (27%) satisfactory with PT alone; 90 (60%) went to surgery; 20 (13%) dropped out.** PT QuickDASH change −15.6 (−29.5%) vs surgery −29.8 (−47.9%), p=.001. |
| Fouasson-Chailloux 2025 | 220 (182 completers) | 3-week inpatient rehab. Rotator strength +13–18%, **rotator endurance +35–39%** on symptomatic side; grip +22%; QuickDASH 57±14 → 30±19; NRS 5.6 → 2.4; sick leave 66% → 43%. All p≤.001. Uncontrolled. |

Lindgren's 88% and Balderman's 27% are not in conflict — they are **opposite ends of a selection spectrum**. Balderman's cohort is a tertiary vascular-surgery referral population pre-selected toward surgical candidacy; Lindgren's is inpatient-rehab-selected with a subjective satisfaction endpoint. Neither is the number for an athlete.

**Is there an RCT of exercise therapy for nTOS? No.**
- **STOPNTOS (Goeteyn 2022)** is the only RCT in nTOS, and it is *surgery vs continued conservative* in patients **already refractory to conservative therapy**. n=50. At 3 months DASH 45.15 (95% CI 38.08–52.21) for surgery vs 64.92 (57.54–72.30) for conservative, p<.001. **All 25 conservative-arm patients applied for surgery at 3 months.** This is evidence that continued conservative care fails in non-responders — not evidence about exercise content.
- Goharinejad 2024 (n=88) randomised *delivery mode* (mobile app vs brochure), not exercise content; only neck-pain NRS differed (p=.024).
- Joshi 2026 (n=110) is a prospective comparative study, not randomised, in Cureus.

No trial has ever randomised nTOS patients to a scapular endurance programme versus a control programme.

### 2. Direct evidence on muscle endurance/capacity in TOS

**The flagship: Daley 2021 (PMID 34573871).** 100 NTOS patients vs 100 healthy controls, prospective. Isokinetic shoulder rotator testing at 60°/s and 180°/s, plus **an endurance test defined as 30 repetitions at 180°/s**.

| Measure | Medial rotators | Lateral rotators |
|---|---|---|
| Peak strength 60°/s | −21% | −29% |
| Peak strength 180°/s | −23% | −20% |
| **Endurance (30 reps @180°/s)** | **−45%** | **−30%** |

All p≤.001; all correlated with QuickDASH (patient mean QuickDASH 58.3±13.9). The endurance deficit is roughly **twice** the strength deficit — the most striking number in this entire sweep.

**Four constraints that block a causal reading, and you must state all four:**

1. **Direction of causation is unresolvable by this design.** NTOS *is* brachial plexus compression. Reduced fatigue resistance is at least as plausibly a *consequence* (partial denervation, pain inhibition, disuse, kinesiophobia) as a cause. A cross-sectional symptomatic-vs-control design cannot separate these. The authors make no causal claim; they frame it as a diagnostic and follow-up tool.
2. **Wrong muscles.** This measured **glenohumeral rotators** — not scapular stabilisers, not deep neck flexors, not postural muscles. The brief's specific question is about a different muscle group.
3. **Wrong population.** 71% female, mean age 39.4±9.6, clinic population. **This has never been measured in an athlete.** Its transfer to a 20-year-old male pitcher is assumption, not data. The same applies to Fouasson-Chailloux 2021 (73% female, 40.4 yr), Saglam 2020, Balderman 2019, Lindgren 1997 and Novak 1995 — **every direct capacity study in TOS is a non-athlete, predominantly female, ~40-year-old clinic cohort.**
4. **The hand-strength companion study argues for consequence.** Fouasson-Chailloux 2021: grip −30%, key pinch −19.5% vs controls. Grip and pinch weakness is the classic C8–T1 lower-plexus signature. That pattern points to nerve compression producing weakness, not weakness producing compression.

**Scapular stabiliser endurance/strength in TOS vs controls: no study exists.** I searched for it directly and found nothing. Scapular winging and dyskinesis appear *descriptively* in TOS cohorts (Burton 2024 — adolescent athletes with scapular winging/dyskinesis and normal EDX who recovered rapidly after decompression; Nordback 2024 "scapular elevation sign") but nobody has measured scapular muscle endurance in a TOS population against controls.

**Deep neck flexor endurance in TOS: zero studies.** A targeted search for TOS + deep neck flexor / craniocervical flexion returned **no results**. This is a complete evidentiary blank. Any claim linking DNF endurance to TOS is extrapolation from the neck-pain literature.

**Respiratory pattern — the evidence is thinner than the theory.** Saglam 2020 (62 TOS vs 47 controls) found TOS patients had significantly lower peak expiratory flow, MIP, MIP%, MEP, MEP%, **and respiratory muscle endurance** (time at 35% MIP to voluntary exhaustion). 74.2% of TOS patients fell below the control 95% CI lower bound for MIP (97.05–113.88 cmH₂O); 85.2% fell below it for MEP (124.74–146.49 cmH₂O). All other spirometry was normal.

**But note carefully what this study did *not* do.** It did not measure scalene EMG. It did not measure apical vs diaphragmatic breathing pattern. It did not show scalene overactivity. It measured *global* respiratory muscle strength and endurance, and found it *reduced* — which, if anything, is the opposite of the "hyperactive accessory breathing muscles" story. The authors explicitly decline a causal direction: *"Trunk muscles perform both postural and breathing functions. Therefore, disruption in one function may negatively affect the other."*

**The specific proposed chain — scalene overuse as an accessory breather → interscalene narrowing → nTOS — has no direct supporting study.** It is a physiologically coherent hypothesis that appears in narrative reviews and clinical texts. It has not been tested.

**One genuinely supportive anatomical finding:** Demirbag 2007 imaged 29 TOS patients and 12 controls by MRI in neutral and provocative positions, measuring the interscalene triangle, costoclavicular space, and retropectoralis minor space. Positional change was significant in patients (p<.05) and absent in controls, and patients differed from controls in the magnitude of positional change (p<.05). Minimum costoclavicular distance differed between patients with positive vs negative Halsted manoeuvre. **This proves the outlet spaces are real, measurable, and position-dependent.** It says nothing about muscular endurance.

### 3. Fatigue → scapular kinematics (where the real evidence lives — with a caveat)

This is the strongest and most replicated body of evidence in the sweep. It is also entirely in healthy subjects, acute lab fatigue, framed around subacromial impingement.

| Study | n | Fatigue protocol | Scapular result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tsai 2003 | 30 healthy | External rotation | Less posterior tilt (to 90°), less external rotation (to 120°), **less upward rotation** (to 60°). Change in posterior tilt correlated with fatigue amount, r = .39–.60. |
| Ebaugh 2006 (JOSPT) | 20 healthy | External rotation | Less posterior tilt early; **more upward rotation** mid-range; more clavicular retraction; less humeral ER. |
| Ebaugh 2006 (JEK) | 20 healthy | Repetitive overhead elevation | **More upward and external rotation**; more clavicular retraction; less humeral ER. All muscles except lower trapezius showed EMG fatigue. |
| Joshi 2011 | 25 overhead athletes | GH external rotation | ↓ lower trapezius activity, ↑ infraspinatus activity, **↑ scapular upward rotation**. |
| Harrison 2021 | 30 | Serratus anterior | ↓ posterior tilt at 60–90° and 90–120°, ↑ scapular internal rotation, ↑ clavicular elevation, **no change in upward rotation**. |

**Two honest observations the brief needs:**

- **What replicates is decreased posterior tilt (i.e. increased anterior tilt).** Four of five studies show it. Combined with Harrison's increased internal rotation, this is the consistent fatigue signature.
- **Upward rotation does not replicate.** Tsai found it decreased; both Ebaugh papers and Joshi found it *increased*; Harrison found no change. The brief's framing ("decreased upward rotation") is only supported by one of five studies. **Do not assert a consistent upward-rotation deficit.**

**The pec minor link is separate and stronger for a different reason.** Borstad & Ludewig 2005 (n=50 pain-free) divided subjects by normalised pec minor resting length. The short group *"stayed anteriorly tipped at higher angles"* and showed a *"more internally rotated scapula."* This is the actual evidentiary basis for pec minor lengthening in TOS protocols — and it is about *resting muscle length*, not endurance or fatigue.

**Throwing/pitching-specific fatigue:** Grantham 2014 followed 11 NCAA D1 pitchers across 26 live games (mean 97.2±16.1 pitches/start, 1079±251/season). Hip lean at hand separation, elbow height at foot contact, and maximum shoulder external rotation were the parameters most sensitive to inning, game, and season fatigue. **Note: no scapular measures were taken.** Mine 2025 examined upper-trunk rotation kinematics and arm fatigue after repetitive pitching. Laudner 2008 found lower trapezius strength explained 53–56% of scapular upward rotation variance in 24 professional pitchers (r²=.56 at 90°, .53 at 120°), while serratus anterior relationships were all poor.

**Burkhart, Morgan & Kibler 2003 (SICK scapula)** — the field's canonical description of scapular malposition in throwers, and the origin of "inferior medial border prominence, coracoid pain, dyskinesis." **It is expert opinion with no abstract in the bibliographic record.** Cite it as a conceptual framework, not as evidence.

**THE INFERRED LINK — label it clearly as inferred.** The chain is:
> scapular muscle fatigue → increased scapular anterior tilt and internal rotation (measured, replicated) → the coracoid moves inferoanteriorly and the clavicle approaches the first rib (anatomically reasoned) → narrowing of the costoclavicular and retropectoralis minor spaces (spaces are real and position-dependent per Demirbag 2007, but never measured under fatigue) → brachial plexus compression (never demonstrated)

**The critical missing experiment: no study has ever measured costoclavicular or retropectoralis minor space before and after a fatigue protocol.** That single study would convert this from plausibility to mechanism. It has not been done. Every study in the table above framed its outcome as *subacromial* space and impingement — not the thoracic outlet.

### 4. Validated field tests a strength coach could use

**Deep Neck Flexor Endurance Test** (Domenech 2011, n=126 asymptomatic adults):
- **Men 38.9 ± 20.1 s; women 29.4 ± 13.7 s** (gender effect F=8.643, p=.004)
- Age (20–80) and activity level did **not** affect performance
- **Inter-rater reliability ICC(2,k) = 0.66 (95% CI 0.34–0.86)** — only moderate, with a CI that reaches down to poor
- Authors flag *"the variability between subjects' DNF endurance capabilities was high"*
- Jarman 2017 adds adolescent/young-adult norms (values not extracted)

**Scapular Muscle Endurance (SME) test** (Edmondston 2008, isometric endurance tests in postural neck pain, n=21):

| Test | ICC | SEM | Minimal detectable change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Neck flexor | 0.93 | 6.4 s | 17.8 s |
| **Scapular** | **0.67** | **10.9 s** | **30.1 s** |
| Neck extensor | 0.88 | 25.9 s | 71.3 s |

**The scapular test's MDC of 30.1 s is large relative to typical hold times — it is not a good instrument for tracking an individual athlete's change.** Use it as a group screen at best.

The SME test discriminates between groups: Eraslan 2013 (91 textile workers, 43 with chronic shoulder pain vs 48 without) found significantly lower SME in the pain group with a significant negative correlation to pain intensity. Sözlü 2024 (23 rotator-cuff-related shoulder pain vs 23 age-sex-matched controls) found lower SME in patients, correlated with FIT-HaNSA function. **No normative values for the SME test were found in this sweep.**

**CKCUEST:** Roush 2007 established reference values in 77 male collegiate baseball players aged 18–22 (15-second touch count, mean of 3 trials, no differences by playing position). Assef 2025 provides NCAA American football reference values. **The actual numeric reference values are in tables not accessible via the bibliographic record.**

**Upper Quarter Y-Balance Test:** Butler 2014, 48 HS baseball + 17 HS softball players, normalised to arm length (%AL):
- Medial: non-throwing 98.4±8.6, throwing 99.1±8.6 (p=.42)
- Inferolateral: 90.8±11.8 vs 90.3±11.5 (p=.61)
- Superolateral: 70.6±10.9 vs 70.4±11.1 (p=.91)
- Composite: 87.2±8.9 vs 86.6±8.1 (p=.72)
- No throwing/non-throwing asymmetry, no sex difference. Schwiertz 2021 gives youth 10–17 norms.

**The decisive caveat for all four tests: not one has ever been validated against TOS.** None has been administered to a TOS population, none has an established cut-point for TOS risk, and CKCUEST and UQYBT are predominantly closed-chain stability/mobility tests rather than endurance tests. A strength coach can use them as general upper-quarter capacity monitoring with defensible normative data. Presenting any of them as a TOS screen would be unsupported.

### 5. Do S&C programmes reduce shoulder injury in overhead athletes?

**The honest answer is "mixed, and weaker than the field believes."**

**The risk-factor case (Clarsen 2014):** 206 elite male handball players, prospective across a 30-week season. Average shoulder-problem prevalence 28% (95% CI 25–31); substantial problems 12% (11–13). Significant associations:
- **Obvious scapular dyskinesis: OR 8.41 (95% CI 1.47–48.1)** — note the enormous, barely-excluding-1 confidence interval
- Total rotational motion: OR 0.77 per 5° (0.56–0.995)
- **External rotation strength: OR 0.71 per 10 Nm (0.44–0.99)**

**The replication failed.** Andersson 2018, same research group, mixed-sex cohort of 329 elite handball players — title: *"previous findings could not be confirmed."* This is a serious problem for anyone building a case on Clarsen 2014 alone.

**The intervention case (Andersson 2017):** 45 teams / 660 players, cluster-randomised, one 7-month season. The OSTRC Shoulder Injury Prevention Programme targeted *"glenohumeral internal rotation, external rotation strength and scapular muscle strength, as well as improve kinetic chain and thoracic mobility,"* delivered by coaches 3×/week in warm-up.
- Shoulder problems: 17% (16–19) intervention vs 23% (21–26) control. **OR 0.72 (0.52–0.98), p=.038**
- **Substantial** shoulder problems: 5% vs 8%. OR 0.78 (0.53–1.16), **p=.23 — not significant**

So the flagship RCT reduced *any* shoulder problem by a modest margin and did **not** significantly reduce the problems that actually cost participation.

**The mechanism failed to move (Fredriksen 2021):** An RCT of exactly the thing these programmes assume — 92 youth handball players, 8 weeks of ER band strengthening (2 exercises, 3×/week, 5–10 min). Between-group difference in dominant-shoulder ER strength: **0.06 N/kg (95% CI −0.01 to 0.14)**. ER:IR ratio difference 0.03 (−0.02 to 0.08). Conclusion: *"The ER strength program improved neither the ER strength nor the ER:IR ratio."* If the dose in a warm-up programme cannot change the strength variable, the mechanistic story is in trouble.

**The pooled evidence is null (Yonneau 2025):** 5 RCTs, 1872 players; 3 pooled, n=747. **OR 0.73 (95% CI 0.45–1.17)** — not significant. *"This study did not demonstrate the effectiveness of prevention programmes for handball shoulder injuries."*

**Baseball's positive RCT used different content (Sakata 2019):** 16 teams / 237 players aged 9–11, block-randomised, 12-month follow-up. Injury incidence 1.7 vs 3.1 per 1000 athlete-exposures; **HR 1.940 (95% CI 1.175–3.205), p=.010** (favouring the intervention). Ball speed also improved (p=.010), and shoulder horizontal adduction deficit, non-dominant hip IR, and thoracic kyphosis angle all improved. **The intervention was 5 stretching + 2 dynamic mobility + 2 balance exercises — no scapular strengthening or endurance work.** The clearest positive trial in baseball did not use the mechanism this brief is interested in.

**Finally, for the athlete-TOS population specifically:** the literature is overwhelmingly surgical. Funakoshi 2024 reports 91.1% excellent/good Roos scores after endoscopy-assisted first-rib resection in 79 overhead athletes (vs 62.8% in 102 non-athletes). Troyer 2023 states flatly that *"Treatment of nTOS generally requires surgical intervention."* Chauhan 2024 covers return to play after surgery in professional baseball. Colbert 2022 is the only athlete-specific rehabilitation paper and it is a **single case report, Level V expert opinion** (a collegiate thrower returning at 18 weeks). **No cohort anywhere reports what fraction of throwing athletes with nTOS resolve with rehabilitation alone.** For a strength-and-conditioning audience, that is the most important absence in the entire literature.

## EVIDENCE STRENGTH VERDICT

**(a) Direct causal evidence that a deficit in scapular, deep-neck-flexor, or postural muscle endurance contributes to TOS: none. Zero. Not weak — absent.** There is no prospective study in any population that measured muscular capacity at baseline and observed who subsequently developed TOS. There is no study that has measured scapular stabiliser endurance in TOS patients versus controls. There is no study of any kind measuring deep neck flexor endurance in a TOS population. There is no study measuring costoclavicular or retropectoralis minor space before and after a fatigue protocol. The four load-bearing experiments that would establish this claim have simply not been run.

**(b) Treatment-implies-mechanism reasoning is the strongest strand, and it is genuinely suggestive but structurally circular.** Daley 2021 is a real, well-powered finding: 100 vs 100, a 45% rotator endurance deficit that exceeds the strength deficit and correlates with disability. Fouasson-Chailloux 2025 shows that endurance improves 35–39% alongside a QuickDASH drop from 57 to 30 with rehabilitation. Saglam 2020 shows reduced respiratory muscle endurance in TOS. O'Sullivan 2026 confirms that virtually every published protocol targets the scapula, trapezius, serratus anterior, scalenes and pec minor. But three things gut the causal inference. First, **NTOS is by definition brachial plexus compression, so reduced fatigue resistance is at least as plausibly a consequence as a cause** — and the companion finding of grip and pinch weakness in a C8–T1 distribution actively favours the consequence reading. Second, **every one of these studies measured glenohumeral rotators, hand grip, or global respiratory muscles — never the scapular stabilisers or deep neck flexors the brief asks about.** Third, **every one was done in a ~40-year-old, 70–90% female clinic population; none has been measured in an athlete.** And the protocols themselves cannot even be interrogated for whether they prescribe endurance, because — in the scoping review's own words — reporting of treatment intensity is poor. Treatment content tells you what clinicians believe, not what causes the disease.

**(c) Pure plausibility carries the rest, and it is well-built plausibility.** Fatigue demonstrably alters scapular kinematics: increased anterior tilt is replicated across four of five protocols and increased internal rotation is shown after serratus fatigue, with Borstad showing that a short pec minor produces the same posture at rest. The outlet spaces are real, measurable, and position-dependent (Demirbag 2007). Anterior tilt plus internal rotation plus depression plausibly narrows the costoclavicular and subcoracoid corridors. But every link past the kinematics is inference: not one fatigue study measured the thoracic outlet, all framed their outcomes around subacromial impingement, all were acute lab protocols in healthy subjects, and the upward-rotation direction the brief assumed is contradicted by three of the five studies. Meanwhile the supporting prevention literature is shakier than commonly presented — the Clarsen risk factors failed to replicate in the same group's own follow-up, the ER-strength mechanism did not move in a dedicated RCT, the pooled handball meta-analysis is null (OR 0.73, 0.45–1.17), the flagship RCT was non-significant for substantial problems, and the one clearly positive baseball RCT used mobility and balance work rather than scapular strengthening.

**The defensible position for the brief.** Say that conservative management is the accepted first line for nTOS and is built around scapular control, postural correction, and scalene/pec minor lengthening; that a large cross-sectional study found a striking rotator endurance deficit in nTOS patients whose direction of causation is unresolved; that fatigue is proven to alter scapular position in ways that would plausibly narrow the outlet; and that **the specific claim "building scapular and postural muscle endurance protects a thrower against TOS" is a reasonable, mechanistically coherent hypothesis with no direct empirical support.** It is worth acting on because the intervention is low-cost, low-risk, and independently justified by general shoulder health — not because the evidence establishes it. Anyone who presents this as established causation is overstating the literature by a wide margin. The most useful honest line for a coaching audience: *nobody has published what fraction of throwing athletes with nTOS resolve with rehabilitation alone.*

---

## COULD NOT VERIFY

1. **"Vicenzino" as an author on the Watson TOS series.** Incorrect. The authors are Watson LA, Pizzari T, Balster S (Man Ther 2009 and 2010).
2. **"Sakthi-Velavan" as an author on Hooper et al.** Incorrect. Authors are Hooper TL, Denton J, McGalliard MK, Brismée JM, Sizer PS. The title is "…a controversial clinical condition. Part 2: non-surgical and surgical management," JMMT 2010;18(3):132-138.
3. **Vanti et al. as a "systematic review."** It is a literature review (Eura Medicophys 2007). It explicitly reports finding no RCTs, systematic reviews or meta-analyses, and its included studies span 1983–2001.
4. **The Edgelow protocol.** No peer-reviewed primary source found in PubMed or Europe PMC under Edgelow or "neurovascular entrapment management." It appears in the field as a textbook chapter (Edgelow PI, in Donatelli RA, *Physical Therapy of the Shoulder*), which I could not verify through a bibliographic database. **Do not cite it as peer-reviewed.**
5. **A Cools et al. study of scapular muscle fatigue in overhead athletes.** Targeted searches returned only Alibazi 2017 (Cools as co-author, on joint hypermobility) and Fredriksen 2021 (Cools as co-author, the ER strength RCT). I could not verify a Cools-first-author scapular-fatigue paper matching the brief's description.
6. **Any RCT of exercise therapy versus control for nTOS.** Does not exist. STOPNTOS is surgery vs continued conservative in refractory patients; Goharinejad tested delivery mode; Joshi 2026 is non-randomised.
7. **Any study of deep neck flexor endurance or the craniocervical flexion test in a TOS population.** Searched directly; no results.
8. **Any study measuring scapular stabiliser strength or endurance in TOS patients versus controls.** None found.
9. **Any study measuring EMG evidence of scalene overactivity during breathing in TOS, or apical vs diaphragmatic breathing pattern in TOS.** None found. The "accessory breathing → interscalene compression" chain is untested.
10. **Any study measuring costoclavicular or retropectoralis minor space before and after a muscular fatigue protocol.** None found. This is the decisive missing experiment.
11. **Normative values for the Scapular Muscle Endurance test.** None found. Only between-group comparisons (Eraslan 2013; Sözlü 2024).
12. **Actual numeric reference values from Roush 2007 (CKCUEST, collegiate baseball).** Reported in tables not accessible via the bibliographic record; the abstract states values were calculated but does not print them.
13. **Burkhart, Morgan & Kibler 2003 (SICK scapula) content.** Citation fully verified (Arthroscopy 2003;19(6):641-661, PMID 12861203, DOI 10.1016/s0749-8063(03)00389-x) but the record carries no abstract, so no claim from it was extracted. It is expert opinion regardless.
14. **Protocol dose details in Watson Part 2 and Hooper Part 2** (sets, reps, endurance-vs-strength prescription, inclusion of diaphragmatic breathing or deep neck flexor work). Verified at abstract level only; full text not retrieved. O'Sullivan 2026's synthesis indicates such detail is poorly reported across the nTOS literature generally.
15. **Jarman 2017 deep neck flexor normative values for adolescents/young adults.** Citation verified; numeric values not extracted.

Report delivered. Summary of what I found and did:

**Method:** Verified all 50 citations through the Europe PMC REST API (serves the MEDLINE/PubMed record — title, authors, journal, year, volume/pages, PMID, DOI, publisher abstract). Nothing from memory or search snippets.

**Three errors in the brief, corrected:** the Manual Therapy series is Watson/Pizzari/**Balster**, not Vicenzino; the JMMT series is Hooper/Denton/McGalliard/Brismée/Sizer with a different title, no Sakthi-Velavan; Vanti 2007 is a narrative literature review with zero RCTs, not a systematic review.

**The headline finding for the brief's central question:** direct causal evidence that a scapular/deep-neck-flexor/postural endurance deficit contributes to TOS is **absent, not weak**. No prospective capacity→TOS study exists; no study has measured scapular stabiliser endurance in TOS vs controls; zero studies of deep neck flexor endurance in TOS; and nobody has measured costoclavicular or retropectoralis minor space before/after a fatigue protocol — the decisive missing experiment.

**What does exist:** Daley 2021 (PMID 34573871) is the flagship — 100 nTOS vs 100 controls, **45%/30% rotator endurance deficit**, roughly double the strength deficit. But it measured glenohumeral rotators (not the muscles in question), in a 71%-female, ~40-year-old clinic population (never measured in an athlete), and nTOS *is* plexus compression, so the deficit is at least as plausibly a consequence.

**Two findings that will surprise the audience:** (1) O'Sullivan 2026's scoping review confirms the protocols target the right muscles but concludes reporting of treatment intensity is "generally poor" — so the literature cannot tell you whether they prescribe endurance or strength; (2) **no cohort anywhere reports what fraction of throwing athletes with nTOS resolve with rehab alone.** The athlete literature is surgery-dominant.

**Also flagged honestly:** the brief's assumed "decreased upward rotation" after fatigue is contradicted by three of five studies (anterior tilt is what replicates); the Clarsen 2014 risk factors failed to replicate in the same group's own 2018 follow-up; the handball prevention meta-analysis is null (OR 0.73, 0.45–1.17); and the one positive baseball RCT used mobility/balance, not scapular strengthening.
